## Working Papers

### Intergenerational Associations in Reported Offending: The Role of Parental Justice-System Contact

**Status:** PhD thesis chapter / Working paper

This study examines intergenerational associations in reported offending in Chile. It links administrative records for the 2010 birth cohort to parental justice-system records and school information. The main sample contains adolescents with exactly one registered mother and one registered father. The adolescent outcome equals one when an adolescent is named as an alleged offender in a report received between 1 January 2024 and 31 March 2025, provided that the adolescent was at least 14 years old on the offense date. Parental reported-offense histories are measured through the day immediately preceding the child's 14th birthday.

Using Linear Probability Models with fixed effects, I estimate conditional associations. Any parental reported-offense history is positively associated with adolescent justice-system contact. The association increases across parental-report-count quartiles and is larger for legally more severe recorded offenses. The most recent parental offenses at ages 11--13 display the largest last-exposure association, although timing may also proxy for persistence. Associations are systematically larger for boys, and the largest parent-source estimate corresponds to histories involving both registered parents. An offense associated with a recorded custodial sentence has a larger coefficient than a report without such a sentence. Finally, multiple-type parental histories have the largest typology estimate. VIF-only histories are not more strongly associated with the outcome than non-VIF-only histories, and the drug-related category is predominantly composed of multiple-type records.
